core: Computational thinking (CT) is a thought process for framing problems so that a computer, or a person, can carry out the solution; it is a way of thinking, not the act of coding.
The term was popularized by Jeannette M. Wing in her 2006 Communications of the ACM Viewpoint, 'Computational Thinking' (Vol. 49, No. 3, pp. 33-35).

Wing's framing: CT builds on the power and limits of computing processes, whether executed by a human or a machine, and is 'a fundamental skill for everyone, not just for computer scientists' that should be added to reading, writing, and arithmetic.
The four widely-taught pillars of CT as presented in CS education: decomposition, pattern recognition, abstraction, and algorithm design (algorithmic thinking).
Decomposition: breaking a complex problem into smaller, more manageable sub-problems that can be analyzed and solved separately.
Pattern recognition: identifying similarities, trends, and recurring structures within or across problems so past solutions can be reused.
Abstraction: focusing on the essential, relevant details of a problem and filtering out the rest to make it tractable.
Algorithm design: expressing a solution as an ordered, step-by-step sequence of unambiguous instructions that a human or computer can follow.
A concrete everyday worked example that applies all four pillars to a non-programming task (planning a Saturday of errands).
CT is distinct from programming: it is the underlying problem-formulation skill, applicable across disciplines, that coding can then implement.
supporting: The 'four pillars/cornerstones' enumeration is a CS-education framing (used by ISTE/CSTA, BBC/CAS, and OER texts), not a verbatim list from Wing's 2006 paper, which describes CT more broadly (recursion, abstraction, decomposition, separation of concerns, choosing representations, reformulating hard problems into solvable ones).
ISTE frames CT as a cross-curricular, for-all-students skill distinct from coding, with core components including decomposition, data analysis, abstraction, and algorithm design.
Abstraction and decomposition are named here as pillars but their depth is owned by sibling topics; this lesson is the overview that ties the pillars together.
outOfScope: The mechanics and deep treatment of decomposition (owned by computer-science-fundamentals:foundations:decomposition).
The mechanics and deep treatment of abstraction (owned by computer-science-fundamentals:foundations:abstraction).
How to design, analyze, and reason about algorithms in depth, and Big-O complexity (owned by computer-science-fundamentals:foundations:algorithms).

Any specific programming language syntax; CT is language-agnostic and pre-code.

claims.claim: The term 'computational thinking' was popularized by Jeannette M. Wing in a 2006 Communications of the ACM Viewpoint article titled 'Computational Thinking' (Vol. 49, No. 3, March 2006, pp. 33-35).

Wing describes computational thinking as 'a fundamental skill for everyone, not just for computer scientists,' arguing that 'to reading, writing, and arithmetic, we should add computational thinking to every child's analytical ability.'

Wing states that computational thinking 'builds on the power and limits of computing processes, whether they are executed by a human or by a machine,' and involves 'solving problems, designing systems, and understanding human behavior, by drawing on the concepts fundamental to computer science' — establishing that CT is a way of thinking rather than the act of programming.

Wing identifies 'using abstraction and decomposition when attacking a large complex task or designing a large complex system' as a central part of computational thinking, and characterizes CT as 'reformulating a seemingly difficult problem into one we know how to solve.'

In CS education, computational thinking is commonly taught through four pillars: decomposition (breaking a complex problem into smaller, manageable parts), pattern recognition (identifying similarities and recurring structures), abstraction (focusing on essential information while ignoring irrelevant detail), and algorithm design/algorithmic thinking (creating step-by-step instructions to solve the problem).

Computational thinking can be characterized as 'the thought processes involved in formulating problems so their solutions can be represented as computational steps and algorithms,' and applies to everyday, non-programming tasks such as budgeting, planning, and data analysis.

Computational thinking is distinct from coding: ISTE frames CT as a cross-curricular problem-solving skill for all students and educators, with core components such as decomposition, gathering and analyzing data, abstraction, and algorithm design, integrated across subjects rather than being coding instruction itself.

The tidy 'four cornerstones' enumeration is a CS-education framing adopted by bodies such as ISTE/CSTA and used in OER texts, rather than a verbatim four-item list from Wing's 2006 paper, which frames CT more broadly (including recursion, separation of concerns, and choosing appropriate representations).

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether computational thinking is exactly 'four pillars.'
positions: CS-education materials (ISTE/CSTA, BBC/CAS, OER intro texts) commonly teach four cornerstones: decomposition, pattern recognition, abstraction, and algorithm design.

Wing's 2006 originating paper does not present a clean four-item list; it describes CT as a broad family of mental tools (abstraction, decomposition, recursion, reformulation, separation of concerns, choosing representations, and more).
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson teaches the four pillars as the standard, widely-taught framing while explicitly noting that Wing's original vision is broader and that the four-pillar breakdown is a teaching convention, so students are not misled into thinking Wing enumerated exactly four.

unsupportedExistingClaims: The generated draft was generic boilerplate ('Computational Thinking is a foundational concept in Computer Science Fundamentals... a simple way to apply it') with no substantive content; all of it was discarded.

Kept the deep mechanics of decomposition, abstraction, algorithms, and pseudocode out of scope, deferring them to their sibling topics; this topic is the overview.

sourceRecords.title: Computational Thinking (Viewpoint)
sourceRecords.provider: Jeannette M. Wing, Communications of the ACM, Vol. 49, No. 3
sourceRecords.notes: The originating article that popularized the term. Canonical record is the ACM Digital Library DOI (10.1145/1118178.1118215); I read the author/CMU-hosted PDF copy at https://www.cs.cmu.edu/~15110-s13/Wing06-ct.pdf on 2026-08-19 (extracted text from the PDF). Verified direct phrasing used to ground the lesson: 'Computational thinking builds on the power and limits of computing processes, whether they are executed by a human or by a machine'; 'Computational thinking is a fundamental skill for everyone, not just for computer scientists. To reading, writing, and arithmetic, we should add computational thinking to every child's analytical ability'; 'Computational thinking involves solving problems, designing systems, and understanding human behavior, by drawing on the concepts fundamental to computer science'; 'Computational thinking is using abstraction and decomposition when attacking a large complex task or designing a large complex system'; 'Computational thinking is reformulating a seemingly difficult problem into one we know how to solve'; and the subtitle 'It represents a universally applicable attitude and skill set everyone, not just computer scientists, would be eager to learn and use.' Treated as REFERENCE_ONLY (ACM copyright); only brief attributed quotations used.

sourceRecords.notes: OpenStax OER, read 2026-08-19. Characterizes computational thinking as 'the thought processes involved in formulating problems so their solutions can be represented as computational steps and algorithms,' credits Jeannette Wing's 2006 paper with bringing CT to prominence, and defines the four pillars: decomposition (breaking a complex problem into smaller, manageable parts), pattern recognition (identifying similarities and recurring structures), abstraction (focusing on essential information while ignoring irrelevant details), and algorithmic thinking (creating step-by-step instructions to solve problems). Gives everyday examples (budgeting, traffic-accident data analysis, planning a community garden, instructing a robot to make a sandwich).
